name: Manx
confidence_why: Broderick 1984, Green 1997 and Lewin 2020 all put Manx stress on the first syllable by default, but all three also describe a regular class of words in which a long second syllable draws the stress (mooarane, jarrood, the -ane/-age/-eyr suffixes and Anglo-Norman loans), so the default placement is secure while the 'strictly initial' label overstates what the sources say.
catalog_quote: Words with all light syllables (including the bégan type that had been (L H) in EMI) maintained initial stress. (73) Manx stage 2: initial stress in all-light words: a. bégan 'a little' b. bánaxən 'blessings'
sweep_summary: Manx (manx1243) is in the catalog as fixed-strict initial, decided from Green 1997 §4.6.5 ('Words with all light syllables.. maintained initial stress'). this search of works with stress in the title listed three titles. (1) Thomson 1976 (Celtica 11: 255-263) is, per Lewin 2020's characterisation, a short article on the vowel phonology of Thomas Christian's idiolect (Marstrander's 1928 transcriptions); 'stressed' in the title is an environment, not stress placement; no open copy exists (DIAS OJS holds only vols 29-37, DAIR no match, archive.org none) - print only, low priority. (2) Ó Sé 1991 (De Gruyter chapter, doi 10.1515/9783111678658.157) is directly about Manx stress shift vs. vowel shortening and, per Lewin, 'the most detailed treatment of the topic to date' with a quantitative analysis of HLSM II items; it is closed (OpenAlex/S2 closed, De Gruyter WAF-blocked) - paywalled, high priority; Lewin's quotations of it (p. 162: sonorant+voiced clusters behave like long initial syllables; tendencies non-categorical, lexical diffusion) are recorded. (3) Green 1997 was already held by the project (ROA-196) and re-read: the catalog quote is verbatim, but the surrounding passage states the other half of the rule - 'all words with a heavy second syllable showed forward stress' - so Green himself describes an initial-default system with a heavy-second-syllable override inside a two-syllable window. Two first-hand/primary sources already in custody were read and say the same: Broderick 1984 HLSM I §6 ('Stress is usually on the first syllable, but there is a body of words which has stress on the second syllable.. [with original short initial syllable] the stress remains on the first syllable, eg. bʹegan') and Lewin 2020: 96 ('A synchronic long vowel in a non-initial syllable is always stressed'), with lexical exceptions in both directions listed at Lewin §5.1.5.2. Best new statement: Broderick 1984 §6, a native-speaker-based primary description that should replace Green's diachronic OT reconstruction as the deciding source. Bearing on the classification: initial default confirmed, but 'fixed-strict' is too strong - the sources describe a quantity-sensitive pattern (initial unless the second syllable has a long vowel, plus final-stressed Anglo-Norman loans); recommend reclassification as initial-default with weight override (window syllables 1-2) or at least flagging the override in the rule. Jenner 1875 (held by the project) is silent.

new_statements.quote: §6. Stress is usually on the first syllable, but there is a body of words which has stress on the second syllable. In this class disyllables which originally had a long vowel initially and finally, eg. (Ir.) fágáil, feasóg, had their stress drawn to the second syllable as a result of shortening of the initial stressed syllable, a point also noticed by Heinrich Wagner. [...] Words having an original short initial syllable do not have a long second syllable in Spoken Manx, and consequently the stress remains on the first syllable, eg. bʹegan (Ir. beagán). As can be seen from the pronunciation the -an is not long in Manx.

new_statements.reading: First-hand description of Late Spoken Manx from the last native speakers: stress falls on the first syllable by default, but a definable class of words (those whose second syllable is long, historically from long-long disyllables such as fágáil, feasóg, or from vocalised medial spirants as in jarrood [dʹaˈruːd]) carries stress on the second syllable; words with an originally short initial syllable have a shortened second syllable and keep initial stress (bʹegan). Lewin 2020: 96 states the same rule synchronically ('Stress usually occurs on the first syllable.. A synchronic long vowel in a non-initial syllable is always stressed'). scanned diacritics normalised (djvu text has fa*ga*il, feasdg, b^gan).

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is on the first syllable by default; a word whose second syllable is (synchronically) long carries the stress on that second syllable, whether the length is historical (Irish long-long disyllables such as fágáil, feasóg) or secondary from vocalisation of a medial spirant (jarrood). Words with an originally short first syllable keep a short second syllable and initial stress (beggan). In synchronic terms: stress the long non-initial vowel if there is one, otherwise the first syllable (cf. Lewin 2020: 96 'A synchronic long vowel in a non-initial syllable is always stressed').
new_statements.exceptions: Footnote **: a second syllable lengthened only by loss of an intervocalic spirant, e.g. 'spɪnaːn 'spoons', keeps initial stress. Broderick refers the fuller treatment to a forthcoming ZCP article. Ó Sé 1991 (per Lewin 2020: 361, held by the project) says the weight conditioning is not categorical (stress shift also in some light-initial words; lexical diffusion); Anglo-Norman loans (shirveish, resoon) have final stress.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe Late Spoken Manx (the speech of the last native speakers recorded c. 1909-1972, Broderick's 'last 30 native Manx speakers'); Lewin 2020 covers Classical/Late Manx historically. No separate dialect is singled out for the stress rule; Broderick notes some northern speakers only for vowel quality, not stress.

readall_conflicts: No disagreement between sources on the facts: Broderick 1984 (HLSM I §6, p. 6), Lewin 2020 (p. 96 §1.7.7; pp. 361-2 §5.1, already held by the project) and Green 1997 (§3.4.2.3 pp. 90-93, already held by the project) all describe initial stress as the default with stress attracted to a long (heavy) non-initial syllable (mooarane /muˈrɛːn/ vs beggan /ˈbeɡan/), and final stress in Anglo-Norman loans. The only tension is with the catalog's classification: StressTyp2 records Manx as fixed: initial syllable, whereas every first-hand source frames the second-syllable-stressed class as conditioned by vowel length, which is weight-sensitivity (Green 1997 models it with WSP; Lewin: 'A synchronic long vowel in a non-initial syllable is always stressed'). Ó Sé 1991 (reported in Lewin 2020: 361; not open) adds that the weight conditioning is not categorical and reflects lexical diffusion, so a small lexically unpredictable residue exists. HLSM vol. 3 pp. 148-153 itself could not be opened.

audit.recode_to: weight (weight-sensitive with a fixed default): default initial stress; a non-initial (in practice second) syllable with a long vowel or diphthong takes the stress ('forward stress': mooarane /muˈrɛːn/, faagail /fəˈgɛːlʲ/, jarrood /dʒaˈruːd/, shirveish, resoon), unstressed long vowels do not survive; heavy = long V / diphthong, left-edge window (Green 1997:133 binary colon). If the catalog prefers to treat the forward-stress vocabulary as a closed lexical class (O Se 1991: tendencies not categorical), then fixed-dominant with a 'heavy'/exception field — but not fixed-strict.

sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: As we saw in chapter 3, at an early stage of Manx, native words had initial stress (70), while Anglo-Norman words had forward stress (71). [...] This pattern was simplified, perhaps gradually, until all words with a heavy second syllable showed forward stress. Unstressed long vowels were shortened in order to comply with the WSP. (72) Manx stage 2: forward stress in all eligible words [...] Anglo-Norman words were no longer lexical exceptions, but behaved like native words. Words with all light syllables (including the bégan type that had been (L H) in EMI) maintained initial stress. (73) Manx stage 2: initial stress in all-light words a. bégan 'a little' b. bánaxən 'blessings'
sources.locator: §4.6.5 'Stress in Manx' pp. 131-133 (txt l.3005-3031); §3.4.2.3 'Manx shortening and stress shift' pp. 90-93 (txt l.2169-2215)
sources.note: This is the catalog's deciding source and the quote is verbatim there. The fuller passage shows the catalog's excerpt is one half of a two-part rule: Late Manx stress is initial in words whose syllables are all light, but 'all words with a heavy second syllable showed forward stress' (d'arú:d, bogé:dn, prizú:dn); Green models this as a binary right-headed colon at the left edge (window: first two syllables). Data are secondary (from Broderick 1984, 1986). Refines: Manx is initial-default with a heavy-second-syllable override, not fixed-strict initial.

sources.citation: Lewin, Christopher. 2020. Aspects of the historical phonology of Manx. PhD thesis, University of Edinburgh.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: 1.7.7 Stress. Stress usually occurs on the first syllable (§5.1). In the transcriptions it is ordinarily only marked if it occurs on a non-initial syllable. A synchronic long vowel in a non-initial syllable is always stressed. [p. 96] ... The situation in Manx is particularly complex in that both solutions are found: some words have stress-shift, while others have retention of initial stress with shortening of unstressed long vowel. [...] there is a strong tendency towards stress shift in items with historical long or 'half-long' vowels (including diphthongs), in the initial syllable, while items with short vowels in the initial syllable are likely to show initial stress with vowel shortening [pp. 361-362]
sources.note: Synchronic rule: initial stress by default; any long vowel in a non-initial syllable is stressed (weight-to-stress). Diachronically the choice between stress shift (mooarane /muˈrɛːn/) and shortening (beggan /ˈbeɡan/) is conditioned by the weight of the historical initial syllable, with lexical exceptions in both directions listed at §5.1.5.2 (aashag, tholtan etc. with initial stress; cliegeen, putage etc. with shift). Anglo-Norman loans (shirveish, resoon) have final stress. Confirms initial default; refines fixed-strict to a quantity-sensitive two-syllable-window system.
